title: Two Indian Teenagers Are One Win From a Wimbledon Junior Main Draw. A Decade Ago, This Was Unthinkable.
excerpt: Maaya Rajeshwaran Revathi, seeded No. 1 in girls' qualifying, and 17-year-old Hitesh Chauhan both reached the final qualifying round at Roehampton — backed by academy training and corporate money that earlier generations never had.
body:
For most of the past two decades, an Indian name in a Wimbledon singles draw meant one thing: Sania Mirza, and then a long, anxious wait for whoever might come next. This week, on the manicured grass at Roehampton, the wait looked a little shorter. India sent a four-strong contingent into the qualifying rounds of the 2026 Wimbledon junior championships, and two of them — 16-year-old Maaya Rajeshwaran Revathi and 17-year-old Hitesh Chauhan — battled their way to the final qualifying round, one win away from a Grand Slam junior main draw.

It is the kind of quiet milestone that does not make the back pages in London but lands hard in living rooms from Coimbatore to California: Indian juniors, no longer turning up just to make up the numbers, but seeded, backed, and expected to win.

## A comeback that announced an arrival

Maaya, seeded No. 1 in the girls' qualifying draw and ranked No. 57 in the world juniors, was the headline act — and she nearly went out in the opening round. Facing China's Shiyu Ye, she dropped the first set 4-6 and slid to 1-4 in the second, staring at an early flight home. What followed was the sort of escape that tends to define young careers. She clawed level at 4-4, edged the second-set tiebreak 7-6, and then held her nerve through a 10-point match tiebreak to win 4-6, 7-6, 10-8 after nearly two hours.

It was not pretty, and that was rather the point. The Coimbatore teenager, who trains at the Rafa Nadal Academy in Mallorca, has spent the last 18 months proving she can do the spectacular — reaching a WTA 125 semi-final in Mumbai at 15, becoming the first player born in 2009 or later to get that deep at that level. The Roehampton win showed she can also do the ugly, grinding work that grass-court tennis demands.

## The boy from the qualifiers

Hitesh Chauhan's path was cleaner. The 17-year-old, seeded 16th, dismantled American Lachlan Gaskell — ranked just inside the junior world's top 100 — in straight sets, 6-4, 6-2, serving sharply and attacking the return on a surface that punishes hesitation. It set up a final-round meeting with Italy's Gabriele Crivellaro for a place in the boys' main draw.

Not everything went India's way. Rethin Pranav Senthil Kumar, drawn against second seed Linus Lagerbohm of Finland, lost in straight sets, and Arnav Vijay Paparkar also exited early. But two of four reaching the final qualifying round, with one seeded at the very top of her draw, is a depth of presence that simply did not exist a decade ago.

## Why this is more than a junior result

The temptation is to file Wimbledon junior qualifying under "promising, ask again later." That would miss what the contingent represents. Maaya is not a one-off prodigy left to fend for herself; she is, in the words of one profile, "a carefully nurtured project." Infosys funds her training at Nadal's academy for two years. She is represented by 72 Sports in partnership with Baseline Ventures — the same stable that manages Andrey Rublev, Alex de Minaur, Elina Svitolina, and Daria Kasatkina.

That scaffolding is the real story. Indian tennis has produced singles talent before and watched much of it stall for want of money, coaching, and international match exposure. The current crop is arriving on the junior Slam circuit with European academy training, corporate backing, and professional management already in place — the infrastructure that converts talent into ranking points instead of into what-might-have-been.

## The diaspora stake

For Indian-American families, this is personal in a way a senior cricket result rarely is. The junior tennis pipeline runs straight through the United States — the US college system, the ITF and junior circuits across Florida and California, the WTA and ATP feeder events that dot the American calendar. Maaya made her Grand Slam main-draw debut at the 2025 US Open in New York, winning her opening round. The next generation of Indian players will be seen, scouted, and often based in the same American cities where the diaspora lives.

When a 16-year-old from Coimbatore wins a nerve-shredding tiebreak at Roehampton, she is also widening a path that diaspora kids picking up rackets in New Jersey or the Bay Area can imagine walking themselves. India's tennis future is being built partly on grass in London and partly on hard courts in America — and for once, the names in the draw suggest the wait for the next Sania may not be a long one.
